Before you build: ten minutes on making your agent stop repeating the same mistakes.

# [Teach Your Agent]{.flow} {.title}

## The friction you know

- One week in, you have corrected your agent on the same things again and again: naming style, the library you prefer, "keep functions short", "round money to two decimals"
- Every session starts from zero: the agent remembers [nothing]{.highlight} between sessions (Session X, the loop)
- Explaining the same thing five times is work you should not be doing

## Package the rules once

- Put your project rules in **one markdown file** in the repo: `AGENTS.md`
- What goes in: what the project is, the tools it uses, naming and style conventions, "any AI use lands in the README disclosure"
- Mistral Vibe reads it at every session start, automatically: write the rules once, stop repeating them

## Skills: instructions on demand

- A **skill** is the next step up: a folder with a `SKILL.md`, holding a name, a description, and instructions
- Rules apply [always]{.highlight}. A skill loads only when the task matches its description, so context stays lean until the moment it is needed
- Example: a `verify` skill for your project: read the diff, run it, test it on a case where you know the answer, report what you checked
- In your stack: `.vibe/skills/verify/SKILL.md` in the repo. Vibe loads it in the terminal and inside Zed's agent panel, same engine
- Vibe follows an open format, so skills you write here also work in other agents that adopt it

## Anatomy, briefly

```markdown
---
name: verify
description: Check changed code the way this project requires. Use after any code change.
---

- Read the diff line by line before running anything
- Run the code on a case where you know the correct answer
- Report what you checked and what the result was
```

. . .

Plain markdown you own, at `.vibe/skills/verify/SKILL.md`, versioned with the project like any other file.

## Write your own

- Any workflow you have explained to the agent [twice]{.highlight} deserves a skill
- Keep it short: a page of instructions, not an essay
- Prune it when the workflow changes: a stale skill misleads
- Downloading one? Vet it by [reading it]{.highlight}, not by how popular it is

## What not to hand over

- The parts you must be able to **defend at the demo**: design choices, the statistics, why this approach
- A file can carry conventions. It cannot carry your judgment, and the demo questions come to you, not to it

# [The Work Menu]{.flow} {.title}

## Today

- **Pull before you start, push when you stop.** GitHub is your backup; commit as you go
- Progress today means one working step pushed to GitHub, with commits that tell the story
- I am in the room: use me for blockers, design questions, and "is this scope realistic?"
- Use the agent where it helps, and note down what it did for your disclosure section

## When you're stuck

:::{.callout-tip}
A red traceback you have never seen? Read the last line first, exactly as in Part I. Then, and only then, the agent.
:::

# [Wrap-up]{.flow} {.title}

## Three things to remember

- Rules in `AGENTS.md` for the [always]{.highlight} stuff, skills for the on-demand stuff, both plain markdown you own
- Any workflow you have explained to the agent [twice]{.highlight} deserves a skill
- Small commits, pushed often, are the cheapest insurance any of you can buy
